title: Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type
authors: Rick Bebon, Aljaž Godec, Angelika Rohde
abstract: Additive functionals $\overline{J}_t=\frac{1}{t}\int_0^tU(X_s)\circ dX_s$ of Stratonovich-type recently attracted much attention in the context of inference of thermodynamic properties of complex systems from observations $U$ of individual fluctuating paths $(X_s)_{0\le s\le t}$, whereby $X_0$ is initiated from some general measure. Concentration results on $\overline{J}_t$, albeit desirable, are virtually nonexistent. They turn out to be significantly more challenging to prove than for classical Lebesgue-type functionals $\overlineρ_t=\frac{1}{t}\int_0^t V(X_s)ds$ because the tilt deforms the full second-order structure of the Feynman-Kac generator instead of contributing an additive potential. This renders the generator generally non-self-adjoint even under detailed balance. We overcome this by working with a symmetrized Dirichlet form with a new effective potential that now couples the observable to the non-equilibrium character of the dynamics. We prove concentration inequalities for $\overline{J}_t$ for any bounded, sufficiently smooth vector-valued function $U$ of a general geometrically ergodic diffusion process $X_s$, including explicit sub-gamma and Bernstein-type inequalities, and we obtain explicit upper bounds on ${\rm Var}(\overline{J}_t)$. Strikingly, under detailed balance the concentration of $\overline{J}_t$ is distinctively sub-Gaussian at all times and all deviations, with a variance proxy fixed by the noise alone and independent of the spectral gap, which has no analog for $\overlineρ_t$.
summary: This paper develops a rigorous, non-asymptotic theory for the concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type, which are crucial for analyzing thermodynamic quantities along fluctuating paths. By employing a novel symmetrization technique, the authors overcome mathematical hurdles associated with non-self-adjoint generators. The results provide powerful, explicit concentration bounds, particularly highlighting a distinct sub-Gaussian behavior under detailed balance.
main_problem: The paper tackles the challenging problem of proving non-asymptotic concentration inequalities for additive functionals of Stratonovich-type ($\mathcal{J}_t$) in the context of stochastic thermodynamics.
main_result: They successfully prove concentration inequalities for $\mathcal{J}_t$ for general geometrically ergodic diffusion processes, notably showing that under detailed balance, the concentration is sub-Gaussian with a variance independent of the spectral gap.
method: The authors overcome the difficulty posed by the non-self-adjoint nature of the tilted generator by working with a symmetrized Dirichlet form and bounding the semigroup norm via the quadratic form.
model_or_system: The analysis applies to general geometrically ergodic diffusion processes ($X_s$) describing fluctuating paths in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics. The comparison is drawn between Stratonovich-type functionals (currents) and classical Lebesgue-type functionals.
key_observables: Additive functionals $\mathcal{J}_t =  rac{1}{t}\int_0^t U(X_s)\circ dX_s$, and their concentration bounds.
important_parameters: The time $t$, the function $U$, and the properties of the underlying diffusion process (e.g., geometric ergodicity, detailed balance).
main_assumptions: The analysis requires working with a symmetrized Dirichlet form and assumes the underlying process is a geometrically ergodic diffusion process.
paper_structure: The paper contrasts the mathematical difficulty of Stratonovich functionals versus Lebesgue functionals, develops a novel symmetrization technique for the generator, proves the general concentration inequality, and finally establishes the distinct sub-Gaussian behavior under detailed balance.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical treatment of path functionals like work or entropy production is central to modern non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, providing tools for quantifying fluctuations beyond simple averages.
